entities.name: PMID:25445003
observations: International observational study using International Nutrition Survey data from 2007–2011 in 90 mechanically ventilated burn patients.
Enteral nutrition was received by 88/90 patients; median initiation was 17 hours after admission; 57% had interruptions, commonly for operations.
Mean deficits were 943 kcal/day energy and 49 g/day protein; 19/90 patients died within 60 days.
After severity adjustment, larger energy and protein deficits were associated with mortality: OR 1.10 per 100-kcal deficit and OR 1.16 per 10-g protein deficit.

entities.name: PMID:32336526
observations: Prospective international multicenter observational study of 283 mechanically ventilated burn patients admitted at least 72 hours to 14 burn ICUs in 2014–2015.
Enteral nutrition was used on 90.5% of patient-days; mean energy adequacy was 64.9% and protein adequacy 65.6%.
Only 35.3% achieved at least 80% of energy requirements and 34.3% achieved at least 80% of protein requirements within 48–72 hours.

entities.name: PMID:39225723
observations: Multicenter multinational observational analysis across 54 burn centers in 18 countries, including 493 adults mechanically ventilated within 72 hours and for at least 7 days.
At 6 months, 336 participants were alive; receiving 25% versus 100% of prescribed calories was associated with higher mortality, adjusted HR 3.89 (95% CI 1.35–11.20).
Protein adequacy was not significantly associated with 6-month mortality or functional outcomes.

entities.name: PMID:21116188
observations: Related multicenter observational study of 153 mechanically ventilated burn patients; 80% started enteral nutrition within 24 hours and 95% within 48 hours.
Early enteral nutrition was associated with shorter ICU stay and lower wound-infection risk, but international participation was not established in the abstract.

entities.name: Small-bowel bleeding
observations: After negative EGD and colonoscopy in a hemodynamically stabilized patient with overt bleeding, video capsule endoscopy is guideline-supported first-line small-bowel evaluation.
Multiphasic CT/CTA is preferred when stable patients have active overt bleeding; catheter angiography is for unstable acute overt hemorrhage.

entities.name: Heyde syndrome
observations: Aortic stenosis with gastrointestinal bleeding from angiodysplasia/angioectasia, often involving acquired von Willebrand syndrome.
The association increases suspicion for small-bowel vascular lesions but does not change the immediate next-test algorithm in a stabilized patient.

entities.name: PMID:26303132 ACG guideline
observations: ACG guideline recommends video capsule endoscopy as first-line small-bowel investigation and recommends multiphasic CT for stable patients with active overt bleeding.

entities.name: PMID:25826168 ESGE guideline
observations: ESGE guideline recommends video capsule endoscopy as first-line evaluation and as soon as possible after overt obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, optimally within 14 days.

entities.name: Video capsule endoscopy
observations: Noninvasive first-line small-bowel test after unrevealing upper and lower endoscopy when the patient is stable and bleeding is not briskly ongoing.

entities.name: CT angiography
observations: Useful for stable patients with active or brisk overt bleeding and rapid localization, but not the default next test after bleeding has stopped.
